# A universal strict unequal-scale gain from source-array interpolation

Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a full-dimensional compact convex body with ordinary centroid zero and volume \(V>0\). Put

\[
\Gamma_d=\left(\frac d{d+1}\right)^d,
\qquad
F_u(t)=\frac{|K\cap\{x:u\cdot x\ge t\}|}{V}
\quad(u\ne0).
\]

All cap masses below are **absolute**, before division by the total source mass. For \(0<r\le s\), define

\[
\Phi_d(r,s)=
\begin{cases}
r,&d=1,\\[2mm]
\displaystyle
\left[r c_d+\frac{s-r}{d-1}(1-c_d)\right]^d,
&d\ge2,\quad r\le s\le dr,\\[2mm]
r^d,&d\ge2,\quad s\ge dr,
\end{cases}
\qquad c_d=(2\Gamma_d)^{1/d}.
\tag{1}
\]

Then for every nonzero \(u\) and every real \(t\),

\[
\boxed{\quad
r^dF_u(t/r)+s^dF_u(-t/s)\ge\Phi_d(r,s).
\quad}
\tag{2}
\]

For \(d\ge2\) and \(s>r\), this is strictly stronger than the smaller-copy bound \(2\Gamma_d r^d\). For \(s\ge dr\), the exact minimum over \(t\), even with \(u\) fixed, is \(r^d\). Dimension one has that exact minimum for every \(s\ge r\). No claim of sharpness is made for \(d\ge2\) and \(r<s<dr\).

The proof uses two saved theorems: the equal-copy paired-tail bound in **candidate 732b11a769399016**, and the joint body-and-center source-array root Brunn--Minkowski theorem in **candidate 239caf8af54c6294**, Sections 1--4. The latter has independent audit **unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)**. The support asymmetry needed for the other interpolation endpoint is proved here without a separate background theorem.

## 1. Elementary centroid support asymmetry

Let \(\ell\ge0\) be affine on \(K\), with maximum \(H>0\) at \(v\in K\). For \(0\le t\le H\),

\[
v+(1-t/H)(K-v)\subseteq K\cap\{\ell\ge t\}.
\]

Indeed, the affine value on the homothetic copy is at least
\((t/H)\ell(v)+(1-t/H)0=t\). Its volume is
\((1-t/H)^dV\), including the zero-volume endpoint \(t=H\).
Layer cake therefore gives

\[
\frac1V\int_K\ell(x)\,dx
\ge\int_0^H(1-t/H)^d\,dt=\frac H{d+1}.
\tag{3}
\]

Fix \(u\ne0\), and write the support interval of \(u\cdot K\) as
\([-a,b]\), where \(a,b>0\) because the centroid is interior. Apply (3) to
\(\ell(x)=b-u\cdot x\). Its average is \(b\), and its maximum is \(a+b\). Hence

\[
a\le db.
\]

Applying the same argument to \(-u\) gives \(b\le da\). The support-function criterion for convex inclusion now yields both equivalent containments

\[
-K\subseteq dK,\qquad K\subseteq-dK.
\tag{4}
\]

Here and below dilations are about the centroid zero. In particular \(0\in K\), and \(rK\subseteq sK\) when \(r\le s\).

## 2. The two endpoint arrays and the exact plateau

Place two source bodies over bases \(-1,+1\), and evaluate their source depth at \((0,0)\). Write \(p_{(A,B)}(0)\) for the infimum of the sum of their ordinary \(d\)-volumes in all containing ambient closed halfspaces. It is a source-array depth, not the depth of the convex hull after inserting any additional integer fibers.

For nonzero continuous normal \(u\), a through-point cap has thresholds \(t,-t\), so its mass on \((rK,sK)\) is exactly \(V\) times the left side of (2). A purely base-normal cap through zero captures one entire endpoint source. Any containing cap can be translated to pass through the candidate without increasing its mass.

The proved equal-copy paired-tail theorem gives

\[
p_{(K,K)}(0)\ge2\Gamma_d V.
\tag{5}
\]

The vertical caps are consistent with (5), since \(2\Gamma_d\le1\).
On the other hand, (4) gives \(dK\supseteq-K\), and thus every nonvertical cap satisfies

\[
\begin{aligned}
|K\cap\{u\cdot x\ge t\}|+
|dK\cap\{u\cdot x\ge-t\}|
&\ge |K\cap\{u\cdot x\ge t\}|+
|-K\cap\{u\cdot x\ge-t\}|\\
&=V.
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}
\]

The second summand in the final line is the volume of
\(K\cap\{u\cdot x\le t\}\). Their shared hyperplane has zero \(d\)-volume. This handles empty, full, supporting, and proper caps with the same closed-boundary convention. Purely base-normal caps have mass at least \(V\), and one of them captures the smaller source alone. Consequently

\[
p_{(K,dK)}(0)=V.
\tag{7}
\]

More generally, if \(s\ge dr\), then \(sK\supseteq-rK\), and the same proof gives

\[
p_{(rK,sK)}(0)=r^dV.
\tag{8}
\]

It also proves the pointwise lower bound (2) in this range. For each fixed \(u\), a sufficiently negative finite \(t\) makes the \(rK\)-cap full and the \(sK\)-cap empty (or a zero-volume supporting face). Thus the scalar infimum is exactly \(r^d\), and is attained at a finite threshold. The same endpoint argument proves the upper bound \(r^d\) for the scalar infimum for every \(r\le s\), without a claim of equality below the plateau.

When \(d=1\), a centered interval satisfies \(-K=K\). Therefore the proof of (8) applies for all \(s\ge r\), giving the separate first line of (1).

## 3. Homogeneous source-array interpolation

For an array \(\mathcal A\) at fixed bases, common continuous scaling gives

\[
p_{c\mathcal A}(cy)=c^d p_{\mathcal A}(y)\qquad(c>0).
\tag{9}
\]

Indeed, the invertible map \((z,x)\mapsto(z,cx)\) bijects containing halfspaces and multiplies each source volume by \(c^d\). The bases and their barycentric coefficients do not change.

The joint source-array theorem, combined with (9), implies for \(\alpha,\beta>0\)

\[
p_{\alpha\mathcal A+\beta\mathcal B}(\alpha y+\beta z)^{1/d}
\ge\alpha p_{\mathcal A}(y)^{1/d}
+\beta p_{\mathcal B}(z)^{1/d}.
\tag{10}
\]

To see this exactly, apply its convex-combination form with parameter
\(\beta/(\alpha+\beta)\), then scale by \(\alpha+\beta\).
Cases with one coefficient zero are the corresponding single-array equality and do not require applying the theorem to a zero-volume body.

Assume now \(d\ge2\) and \(r\le s\le dr\). Set

\[
\alpha=\frac{dr-s}{d-1},\qquad
\beta=\frac{s-r}{d-1}.
\tag{11}
\]

These are nonnegative and obey

\[
\alpha+\beta=r,\qquad\alpha+d\beta=s.
\]

Consequently the **componentwise** Minkowski identity is

\[
(rK,sK)=\alpha(K,K)+\beta(K,dK).
\tag{12}
\]

Both endpoint arrays are evaluated at the same continuous point zero, belonging to their midpoint Minkowski sections. Apply (10), (5), and (7):

\[
\begin{aligned}
p_{(rK,sK)}(0)^{1/d}
&\ge V^{1/d}\left[\alpha(2\Gamma_d)^{1/d}+\beta\right]\\
&=V^{1/d}\left[r c_d+\frac{s-r}{d-1}(1-c_d)\right].
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
\]

Since source depth is the infimum over all caps, (13) proves the asserted pointwise bound for every \(u,t\). No minimizing normal or common minimizing allocation between the two arrays is presumed; the saved array theorem retains a common quantile allocation before taking its infimum.

For \(d\ge2\), the binomial expansion gives
\((1+1/d)^d>2\), so \(0<c_d<1\). Equation (13) is therefore strictly larger than \(r^d c_d^d=2\Gamma_d r^d\) whenever \(r<s\le dr\); the plateau is strictly larger as well. Its value equals \(r^d\) at \(s=dr\), so (1) is continuous at the junction.

## 4. An actual midpoint-fiber consequence

Let an actual convex body have positive \(d\)-dimensional fibers at three distinct integer bases
\(p-v,p,p+v\), where \(v\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}\), and suppose its endpoint fibers contain

\[
a_-+rK,\qquad a_++sK.
\]

Write \(g=(a_-+a_+)/2\), \(q=(r+s)/2\). Convexity ensures that the middle fiber contains \(g+qK\). At the **same actual point** \((p,g)\), every ambient containing cap captures from these three disjoint source fibers at least

\[
\boxed{\quad V\bigl[\Phi_d(r,s)+\Gamma_d q^d\bigr].\quad}
\tag{14}
\]

For a through-point cap with nonzero continuous normal \(u\), the two endpoint thresholds relative to \(a_-\) and \(a_+\) sum to zero. Explicitly, a margin
\(A\cdot(z-p)+u\cdot(x-g)\) gives endpoint thresholds
\(t=A\cdot v-u\cdot(a_--g)\) and \(-t\).
Thus (2) pays the first term of (14), while the middle copy \(g+qK\) contributes at least \(\Gamma_d q^dV\) by ordinary Grünbaum at its own centroid \(g\).

A purely base-normal through-point cap contains the whole middle copy and at least one endpoint copy. Its mass is at least \((q^d+r^d)V\), which is no smaller than (14), since \(\Phi_d(r,s)\le r^d\) and \(\Gamma_d\le1\). Translating a containing cap through the candidate completes the proof for all closed caps.

Additional volume in the actual middle fiber, or in any other fiber, is not assigned an automatic Grünbaum contribution at \(g\). Equation (14) counts only the three stated homothetic subbodies. It is a local compensation estimate; no assertion that such estimates can be summed globally is made.

## 5. Relation to the disproved sharp formulas and checks

The universal interpolation bound does not assert either the midpoint-radius expression
\(\min\{r^d,2\Gamma_d((r+s)/2)^d\}\), disproved in
**candidate 5a9bea64014b6234**, or the exact untruncated two-facet value for every truncated affine-power marginal. The latter is disproved in
**candidate 9fcca2d086b8f393**, including a both-proper-cap counterexample.

The standalone verifier **../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_unequal_pair_source_interpolation.py** checks the homogeneous coefficient identities, both endpoint values, the plateau, and exact finite-frustum profiles against (1). Irrational \(2^{1/d}\) is enclosed by rational integer-root bounds, so the finite checks do not use floating-point evidence. They are diagnostics; Sections 1--4 prove the theorem.
